subject: zoology
question_text: Describe the structure of a skeletal muscle.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.32, SAQ 19). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. FIGURE SCOPE: the question does not ask for a diagram and this book prints none, so the muscle-to-fascicle-to-fibre drawing is authored as a 0-mark study figure, not a mark-bearing step.

steps.label: What a skeletal muscle is
steps.why: The name says where the muscle is attached, and the tendon is the structure that makes the attachment, so both come first.
common_mistakes: Calling the fibres branched. Skeletal muscle fibres are unbranched; cardiac fibres are branched.
Writing that the muscle is attached to bone by a ligament. A ligament joins bone to bone.
steps.memory_tip: Skeletal muscle: attached to the skeleton, by a tendon, and built of long unbranched fibres.
steps.margin_note: Where it is attached, how it is attached, what it is made of. Three lines.
lines: Skeletal muscles are the muscles attached to the
bones of the skeleton.
They are attached to bones by tendons.
A skeletal muscle is built of many long,
cylindrical, unbranched muscle fibres.

steps.label: Diagram — muscle, fascicle, fibre
steps.why: The three sheaths are almost impossible to keep apart in words alone; drawing them once as one inside another fixes which sheath wraps a fibre, which wraps a bundle and which wraps the whole muscle.
common_mistakes: Drawing the perimysium round a single fibre. It wraps a whole fascicle.
Leaving the tendon out. The three sheaths join at the end of the muscle to form it.
steps.memory_tip: Draw from the inside out: fibre, then bundle, then whole muscle, with a sheath at each step.
steps.margin_note: The question does not ask for a diagram, so it earns no mark here. Drawing it is the quickest way to fix the three sheaths in order.

elements.caption: Step 1 — the bone and the tendon
Step 2 — the muscle belly inside the epimysium
Step 3 — three fascicles inside the muscle
Step 4 — one fascicle enlarged, in its perimysium
Step 5 — muscle fibres and the endomysium

steps.label: The three connective tissue sheaths
steps.why: The three sheaths lie one inside another, so learning them in order — fibre, bundle, whole muscle — also gives the order of the parts they wrap.
common_mistakes: Swapping perimysium and epimysium. Peri wraps the bundle; epi wraps the whole muscle.
Calling a fascicle a fibre. A fascicle is a BUNDLE of fibres.
steps.memory_tip: Endo inside one fibre, peri around a bundle, epi over everything — and then all three become the tendon.
steps.margin_note: Three sheaths in order, with what each one wraps. End with the tendon.
lines: Each muscle fibre is wrapped in a thin
connective tissue sheath, the endomysium.
A bundle of muscle fibres is called a fascicle.
Each fascicle is wrapped in the perimysium.
A group of fascicles forms the muscle, and the
whole muscle is wrapped in the epimysium.
At the end of the muscle these three sheaths
come together and form the tendon.

steps.label: Structure of the muscle fibre
steps.why: One muscle fibre is formed by many cells joining together, which is why a single fibre carries many nuclei and why they are pushed out to the edge.
common_mistakes: Writing that the nuclei are central. In skeletal muscle they are peripheral; in cardiac muscle the single nucleus is central.
Calling the cytoplasm sarcomere. The cytoplasm is sarcoplasm; a sarcomere is a unit of the myofibril.
steps.memory_tip: A skeletal fibre has many nuclei, all at the edge; a cardiac cell has one nucleus, in the middle.
steps.margin_note: Shape, nuclei, sarcoplasm, myofibrils. One line each.
lines: A skeletal muscle fibre is a long, cylindrical,
unbranched cell.
It is multinucleate (a syncytium), and its
nuclei lie at the edge, just under the membrane.
Its cytoplasm is called sarcoplasm and holds
many myofibrils.

steps.label: Bands and properties
steps.why: The bands are what the word striated records, and quick contraction with quick fatigue is the property that separates skeletal muscle from cardiac muscle.
common_mistakes: Writing that skeletal muscle does not tire. It fatigues quickly; cardiac muscle is the one that resists fatigue.
Calling it involuntary. Skeletal muscle is voluntary.
steps.memory_tip: Striped, voluntary, quick to act and quick to tire — four words that name skeletal muscle.
steps.margin_note: The bands are the reason for the name. Close with voluntary and quick fatigue.

lines.text: Dark and light bands: striped muscle

lines: Each myofibril shows alternate dark and light
bands, so skeletal muscle is also called
striped or striated muscle.
It is under the control of the will, so it is
voluntary muscle.
It contracts quickly and it tires quickly.

insider_note: The three sheaths are the heart of this answer and the examiner checks them by name and by order; the fibre details are the easy marks that most students write first.
